title: Home and household in Old Testament Israel
premise: The walls of Israelite houses survive and their evenings do not, so a reader must keep what was found apart from what is pictured.
question: What was found on the floor, and what am I picturing?
outcomes: Walk through a pillared house room by room, and say what kind of evidence stands behind each room.
Follow bread from the jar to the table and cloth from the fibre to the bed.
Tell a find from a reconstruction, and both from a passage.
Test a claim about Israelite home life, and say what the evidence can and cannot carry.

boundaries.in: The house and what went on inside it, from the Iron Age to the exile: rooms, food once at the house, clothing, who worked and slept where, who counted as a household.
out: Homes in the first century AD: The world of Jesus & the apostles.
Ploughing, harvest and threshing: the planned study The farming year.
Water supply: the planned study Land, climate and water.
Feasts, courts and health, childbirth among them: their own planned studies.
Household gods and worship at home: the planned study Ugarit and the gods of Canaan.
How a family should be ordered: Scripture's teaching, not an archaeological question. See the Marriage & family topics.

scale.note: An excavation report, or a scholar reporting one, says it was in the ground.
A modern drawing or model puts it there. The source is named.
A passage of Scripture mentions it. Most passages describe one house, not all houses.

rooms.name: The door
rooms.evidence: In the usual plan the inner rooms open straight off a central space, so a visitor comes in through the middle of the house. Scripture speaks of the doorframe and the doorposts of houses.
rooms.inference: The door faced the working part of the house, and from there each room could be reached without crossing another.
rooms.limit: The reports read here do not say how doors were hung. The passages mention doors in passing, or for a purpose of their own.

rooms.name: The middle space
rooms.evidence: One of the four parts was often an unroofed courtyard. Carol Meyers reports that almost half of hundreds of excavated ovens stood in courtyards or open spaces. Scripture names a courtyard at a house in Bahurim.
rooms.inference: The middle of the house was its workroom: fire, grain and shared tasks gathered here, in at least many houses.
rooms.limit: Sources call this space a courtyard and a main room. It varied, and whether a given one had a roof is often not known. One artist's drawing places a hearth, a grinder and a loom here: that is a reconstruction.

rooms.name: The side rooms
rooms.evidence: At Tel Halif a cobbled floor, called area G, is described as likely a stable. Scripture has a fattened calf at a woman's house, and a manger that stands empty without oxen.
rooms.inference: Some side rooms held animals in some houses. The popular drawing, with beasts stalled between pillars at night and warmth rising to the family above, is a reasonable picture of those houses.
rooms.limit: A cobbled floor shows a floor. Pillars are not the mark of this house type and have been confused with storehouses and stables. No test on the floors for animal waste was among the sources read.

rooms.name: The back room
rooms.evidence: A broad room across the rear is what defines the type. Tim Frank's study of Tel Halif reports storage jars beside an oven and a grinding installation, and in small clusters: “The location of storage jars and other items was not random.”
rooms.inference: The back room suited storage, as many drawings show, but stored food was also kept where it was being used.
rooms.limit: Frank warns that what was stored in which container is not well known. His tables of capacity, room by room, are in the part of his book not read here.

rooms.name: The upper floor
rooms.line: An argument more than a room.
rooms.evidence: Few houses stand high enough to show one directly. Tim Frank's book models one Halif house in a “one-storey scenario”, as its list of tables shows, so scholars work with more than one possibility. Scripture names a small room upstairs at Shunem and an upper room at a widow's house.
rooms.inference: Some houses had an upper floor. Where one existed it was probably where people lived, as the usual reconstruction says.
rooms.limit: Upper floors fall into the rooms below, and how many houses had one cannot be counted from the sources read. The woman at Shunem proposes to build her small room for a guest, so it does not show who slept upstairs in an ordinary house.

rooms.name: The roof
rooms.evidence: The law requires a railing around a new roof. Rahab lays out flax on hers. Samuel speaks with Saul on a roof, and calls to him there before dawn.
rooms.inference: Roofs were flat and used. Work was done on them, and at least sometimes a guest slept there.
rooms.limit: No roof survives. One reconstruction describes earth and chalk packed with a roller; that detail comes from the drawing's caption and is not shown from a find here.

tasks.name: Grinding grain

middle.why: One drawing puts the grinder beside the central hearth.

tasks.note: Meyers reports several grinding sets in one house, which she reads as women grinding together.

tasks.name: Baking

middle.why: Almost half of hundreds of ovens stood in courtyards or open spaces.

tasks.note: Where the rest of the ovens stood is not given in the source read.

tasks.name: Cooking stew

middle.why: A hearth or oven in the central room or courtyard, in a standard plan.

tasks.note: Israelite houses had no kitchen in the modern sense.

tasks.name: Weaving

middle.why: One drawing stands a loom beside the entrance to the back room.

tasks.note: Rows of fallen loom weights are how a loom's place is usually found; none is measured on this page.

tasks.name: Storing food
tasks.halif: beside the oven, and in clusters

middle.why: Jars beside an oven and a grinding installation. Ovens are often in the middle, so this study places them here.

back.why: One drawing makes the back room the pantry.

tasks.note: Frank's fuller tables of storage by room are not in the part read.

tasks.name: Stabling animals

side.why: One drawing stalls livestock between the pillars.

tasks.note: Area G's cobbled floor is called likely a stable, in a report of a digital model.

tasks.name: Eating

middle.why: A mat on the floor near the hearth, or in the open courtyard.

upper.why: One drawing has the family eating upstairs.

tasks.disagree: No find read here settles it, and the answer may differ from house to house.

tasks.name: Sleeping

upper.why: One drawing shows a bedroll upstairs. Scripture also has a guest's bed in a small room upstairs at Shunem.

roof.why: Samuel calls to Saul on the roof before dawn, and this study infers Saul slept there.

tasks.note: A poor man's bedding could be the cloak he wore that day.

steps.name: Store
steps.line: Grain was kept in underground silos, indoor compartments, pottery jars, and perhaps sacks and chests.

steps.name: Grind
steps.line: A handstone was pushed back and forth on a concave stone called a saddle quern. Carol Meyers estimates at least 2 to 3 hours a day for a family of six.

steps.name: Knead
steps.line: Flour and water, with salt or oil if there was any. Leavened with a sourdough culture, or unleavened when time was short.

steps.name: Bake
steps.line: Usually a tannur: a small clay cylinder open at the top. Dough was slapped against its hot wall, and came off in minutes.

steps.name: Eat
steps.line: Bread with stew made mostly of lentils and vegetables. The word for bread could also mean food, or a meal.

steps.name: Fibre
steps.line: Wool and flax were the two main fibres, and flax could be laid out on a roof.

steps.name: Spin
steps.line: A spindle, weighted with a small whorl, twisted the fibre into thread.

steps.name: Weave
steps.line: On an upright loom, clay weights kept the warp threads taut. The weights survive; the loom's wood rarely does.

steps.name: Wear
steps.line: Scripture names robes and tunics, and wool and linen. One mother makes a little robe each year.

steps.name: Sleep
steps.line: A cloak taken as a pledge had to be back by sunset, because it might be all a man had to sleep in.

objects.name: Cooking pot
objects.line: Where the hot meal was made.
objects.evidence: The Metropolitan Museum lists a ceramic pot, 10.6 by 13.2 cm, from Lachish, marked Israelite and dated by the museum.
objects.inference: Pots like this one held the stews that Scripture and later comparison suggest were the usual hot meal.
objects.limit: The museum's record gives the site, not the building. It does not say whether this pot came from a house or a tomb.

objects.name: Oil lamp
objects.line: A pinched saucer and a wick.
objects.evidence: A ceramic lamp, 14.1 cm long, from Lachish, marked Israelite and dated by the museum. Scripture joins the lamp to the millstones as the sounds and light of a living town.
objects.inference: After dark a house had this much light.
objects.limit: One lamp does not show how many a house owned. The record does not give the building.

objects.name: Oil jug
objects.line: A small jug for a costly liquid.
objects.evidence: The museum calls this 14 cm jug an oil jug. Scripture's widow keeps “a little oil in a jug”.
objects.inference: A small jug suits a small supply used a little at a time.
objects.limit: “Oil jug” is the museum's name for it. Without testing, the name does not prove what it held. The record does not give the building.

objects.name: Bowl
objects.line: The plain end of the meal.
objects.evidence: A ceramic bowl, 7.8 cm high by the museum's measure, from Lachish, marked Israelite.
objects.inference: Shared or single, a bowl was a basic thing on the mat.
objects.limit: Whether one person or a family ate from a bowl this size is not shown by the bowl. The record does not give the building.

objects.name: Loom weights and weaving tools
objects.line: All that is left of the loom.
objects.date: Iron Age I and II, as the museum's label gives it
objects.evidence: A case at Harvard's museum of the ancient Near East shows a needle, beaters and weights of bone or fired clay, from Shechem and Dothan.
objects.inference: Weaving tools turn up at ordinary sites, so cloth was made close to home.
objects.limit: This is a museum's display, photographed by a visitor. It does not show how the tools lay in the ground, and the weaving's product has not survived with them.

objects.name: Women making flour
objects.line: Not Israel, and later: a picture of the posture.
objects.evidence: A terracotta group, 6.2 cm high, in the Metropolitan Museum: women at grinding stones. It is Cypriot, and it is later than most of this study's houses.
objects.inference: It shows what no Israelite find shows: how the work looked, kneeling at a stone. Tim Frank's article uses the same piece.
objects.limit: It is not evidence of who ground grain in Israel. It is shown for the posture only.

kin.gloss: Scholars often call the third ring the “father's house”, a phrase Gideon uses: “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father's house.” The Berean here says “family”.
kin.clusters: Lawrence Stager's 1985 article is widely cited for house clusters: a son marrying and building beside his father, up to three generations, some 10 to 30 people. Read second-hand, in a magazine summary; the article itself was not read. Small shared-wall town houses are often read as single families, and larger detached ones as extended or wealthy households.
kin.unequal: At Tirzah, one guide reports large, well-built houses on one side of a wall, and small crowded ones on the other. The site's dates are disputed: a 2012 paper re-dates the phase and describes a small settlement. Amos and Isaiah speak of the same distance in words, without naming this town.

sizes.label: 10 to 12 m long, 8 to 10 m wide
sizes.note: Iron I examples, in an encyclopedia entry; the larger figures are drawn

sizes.label: Roughly 50 by 30 feet (about 15 by 9 m)
sizes.note: The caption to a popular drawing

claims.claim: “A four-room house means Israelites lived here.”
claims.head: Characteristic is not proof.
claims.evidence: Hundreds are known, mainly in the hill country, and the name “Israelite house” is in use. Ziony Zevit, as reported in an encyclopedia entry, lists similar houses at Tell Keisan, Tell Abu Hawam, Tell Qasile and Tell esh-Shari'a. Notes to Bunimovitz and Faust's article cite more east of the Jordan.
claims.inference: The form is common at Israelite sites and rare enough elsewhere to be worth noticing. It points, and it does not prove.
claims.limit: A wall carries no name. Where the form came from remains uncertain. Bunimovitz and Faust argue a deeper link between the house and Israelite identity; only the opening of that article was read.

test.question: A dig finds one four-room house at a site with no inscriptions. What can it say?

options.why: The form appears at sites scholars do not call Israelite, so one house cannot establish who lived in it.

options.text: This is a kind of house common at Israelite sites.
options.why: That is what the form can carry. Who lived in it needs other evidence.

options.text: Nothing at all: the plan is meaningless.
options.why: The pattern is real and widely attested. It is suggestive, which is not the same as empty.

claims.claim: “The family lived upstairs, above the animals.”
claims.head: A good picture. Not a finding.
claims.evidence: A popular reconstruction draws it so, and encyclopedia entries repeat it. At Tel Halif a cobbled floor is called likely a stable. Tim Frank models one Halif house with a one-storey scenario. The passages name an upper room in particular houses.
claims.inference: In houses with a second floor and animals, it is a likely arrangement. It should not be stretched to every home in Israel across centuries.
claims.limit: Upper floors collapse. The sources read do not count how many houses had one, or how many stalled animals.

test.question: Someone says: “Every Israelite family slept upstairs.” What does the evidence allow?

options.text: Yes: Scripture and archaeology both say so.
options.why: The passages describe particular upper rooms, and one house was modelled with a single storey.

options.text: Some families in some houses probably did.
options.why: The reconstruction is reasonable where a second floor existed. It is not a rule for all.

options.text: No: there were no upper floors.
options.why: Scripture names upper rooms, and scholars reconstruct them from excavated houses.

claims.claim: “The floor tells us who did the work.”
claims.head: A quern has no name on it.
claims.evidence: Carol Meyers states it plainly: artifacts show how things were made, not who made them. Who did the work is worked out from texts and from comparison with more recent village life. Scripture puts a servant girl at the hand mill and a woman at an oven, and it has Jacob cooking stew.
claims.inference: Scripture and later comparison point to women for much of the daily grinding, baking and weaving, and the tasks were not walled off absolutely.
claims.limit: The floors do not say how a household was led, and this study does not ask them to. Meyers draws conclusions about women's standing in the household; those are hers, argued from more than the floors. How a family should be ordered is taught by Scripture, not settled by a floor plan.

test.question: A house has several grinding stones. What can they say?

options.text: More than one person may have ground grain here.
options.why: That is what several sets suggest. Meyers reads it as women grinding together, using other evidence for the “women”.

options.text: The women of this house ran its economy.
options.why: Stones show work. They do not show who ran what.
Nothing in the stones points to a hired trade.

confusedWords.note: A cobbled floor is a find. A cow standing on it at night is a reconstruction, however likely.
A house is a building. A household is its people, land, animals and goods, and may fill more than one building.
The name is for the plan. Some have more, or fewer, and one part was often open to the sky.
Reports often say tabun for what is closer to a tannur. Cynthia Shafer-Elliott explains the muddle.
An object can show how a task was done. It rarely shows who did it.

reach: This page is a selection: six rooms, eight tasks, six objects. It is not a survey of excavated houses.
No excavation report was read in full. Tel Halif's model is known here from an article reporting it, and its lettered areas could not be mapped onto rooms, so they appear in their own column.
Of the museum objects, the Lachish pieces are chosen from about 30 Iron Age records at the Met. None of their records gives a room.
It stops at the exile, and most of what it reads comes from Judah and the hill country of the 8th century BC or nearby. It should not be stretched to all of Israel at all times.
